title: Leabhar a' Chùraim's entry of the turn
summary: At Taigh na Fèithe Donnchadh mac Thormoid enters the turn of the fleet into Leabhar a' Chùraim under a day after Samhain, a full turning of the moon and more after every other account sets the sailing itself. The gap between the two dates is copied faithfully and explained by no word in the leaf that reaches him.

title: Donnchadh's private count of the Diosal
summary: For his own ledger's convenience, and for no reason he offers anyone, Taigh na Fèithe clerk Donnchadh mac Thormoid begins to number years from An Diosal rather than from a reign, working the count backward through his private book to the turn itself. No one above him asks him to keep it, and he tells no one that he does.

title: Broken tidings come to the harbour-house
summary: Word of the fleet reaches Seann Skell by a boat that does not stay to be questioned. Calum mac Nèill copies the telling that same night in a shaking hand; the letters run smaller toward the leaf's foot, and the copy stops without warning where the telling itself stopped.

title: Two shores, not one
summary: Calum's leaf tells of two separate landfalls reached by hulls that had not held together the whole crossing, whether by storm, purpose, or a quarrel the telling does not say. It gives no word of which households reached which shore, and its torn end settles nothing.

title: The tale kept two ways at once at Inis àrsaidh
summary: The broken telling of two shores reaches the fishing hearths of Inis àrsaidh, which gave more households to the roll than any other place. With no way to know which shore holds which kin, the town keeps both halves of the tale alive together, grieving toward one and hoping toward the other by turns.

title: The tidings copied to An Talla Dearg and Taigh na Fèithe
summary: A fair copy of Calum's leaf goes by rider to Cathair dhearg for the queen's own council; a second copy, made by his son Dòmhnall, goes east to Taigh na Fèithe, where Donnchadh mac Thormoid sets it beside his own four-year-old entry of the turn and finds the silence between them unexplained by either leaf.

title: The council divided over the two shores
summary: At An Talla Dearg the custodians argue whether two landfalls mean the fleet prospered or was scattered, and which of the nineteen or one-and-twenty hulls reached which coast. Queen Beathag hears the whole of it and says nothing, and the council lets the matter drop for the day's ordinary business.

title: The grain ruling settled
summary: A long dispute over grain owed the crown's granaries by the upland shires is settled in the queen's favour, the reeves agreeing at last to a measure put to them in her own hand rather than a steward's.

title: The bridge at Àth shean mended in stone
summary: The cracked middle pier of the bridge at Àth shean, shored with timber since a flood two winters before, is rebuilt in stone by masons from the capital, the last props pulled clear on a morning cold enough to break the river's ice.

title: Mòrag's line struck in the ordinary hand
summary: Between the grain ruling and the bridge, in the same plain hand as either, the queen has Murchadh mac Eòghainn enter that Mòrag nic Dhòmhnaill and her children are struck from the succession, as persons no longer on Dia-thìr. Only the old scribe's pen slows at the shaping of the name.

title: Murchadh sands the leaf
summary: Alone in the near-emptied hall, old Murchadh mac Eòghainn sands the leaf that struck the queen's sister from the roll, the same practised motion he has closed every entry with for forty years, giving away nothing of what lies written beneath the sand.

title: Birth of Raghnall mac Raghnaill
summary: A son, named for his father, is born at Cathair dhearg to Raghnall mac Uilleim, the queen's heir, then seven-and-thirty years old. The boy is Beathag's first grandson and the third of her line under An Talla Dearg's roof.
